guidance.title: Vaginal Bleeding
guidance.summary:
Menstruation , or a period, is a woman's monthly bleeding. Abnormal vaginal bleeding is different from normal menstrual periods. It could be bleeding that is between periods, is very heavy, or lasts much longer than usual. It also includes bleeding that happens before puberty or after menopause. Causes can include: 
 Uterine fibroids or polyps 
 Hormone problems 
 Hormone pills, such as birth control pills and hormone therapy for menopause 
 Cancer of the cervix , ovaries , uterus or vagina 
 Thyroid problems 
 

 Bleeding during pregnancy can have several different causes. It is not always serious, but to be safe you should contact your health care provider right away. 

 Pelvic exams, blood tests, imaging tests , and other procedures can help your health care provider diagnose the problem. Treatment depends on the cause. Treatments may include medicines, hormones, and surgery.

guidance.title: Threatened Abortion / Miscarriage
guidance.summary:
**Definitions and Classification:**
Early pregnancy loss (miscarriage) refers to nonviable intrauterine pregnancy up to 13 weeks 0 days gestational age. Classification by clinical presentation:

- **Threatened abortion (O20.0):** Vaginal bleeding with closed cervical os and viable intrauterine pregnancy (IUP) on ultrasound. Fetal cardiac activity present. Occurs in 20-25% of all pregnancies; approximately 50% will progress to pregnancy loss.
- **Inevitable abortion:** Vaginal bleeding with open (dilated) cervical os. Membranes may be intact. Pregnancy loss is imminent or unavoidable.
- **Incomplete abortion:** Partial expulsion of products of conception (POC). Open os, ongoing bleeding, retained tissue on ultrasound.
- **Complete abortion:** Complete expulsion of all POC. Bleeding diminishing. Os closing or closed. Empty uterus on ultrasound with prior confirmed IUP.
- **Missed abortion / embryonic demise (O02.1):** Nonviable pregnancy retained in utero. Closed os, minimal or no bleeding. Diagnosed on ultrasound (absent fetal cardiac activity or anembryonic gestation).
- **Spontaneous abortion, unspecified (O03.9):** Completed pregnancy loss without further specification.

**Incidence:** 15-20% of clinically recognized pregnancies end in spontaneous abortion. The true rate including preclinical losses is 30-50%. Most occur in the first trimester (< 13 weeks).

**Risk Factors:**
- Advanced maternal age (risk doubles from age 20 to age 35; exceeds 50% after age 45)
- Prior miscarriage (recurrent loss defined as 3 or more consecutive losses)
- Chromosomal abnormalities (cause 50-60% of first trimester losses; most common: trisomies, monosomy X, triploidy)
- Uterine anomalies (septate uterus, fibroids, Asherman syndrome)
- Uncontrolled diabetes or thyroid disease

guidance.title: Ectopic Pregnancy
guidance.summary:
1. **Failing to check a pregnancy test.** Every reproductive-age female (roughly 12-55) with abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, syncope, or hypotension needs a pregnancy test. guidance.title: Threatened Abortion / Miscarriage
guidance.summary:
**Threatened Abortion (Viable IUP, Closed Os):**
- **Expectant management** is standard. No intervention has been proven to prevent progression to miscarriage.
- **Progesterone:** The PRISM trial (Coomarasamy 2019, NEJM) showed no significant benefit of vaginal progesterone for threatened miscarriage overall (75% vs 72% live birth rate, p=0.08). A subgroup with history of >= 3 prior miscarriages showed benefit (72% vs 57%). Routine progesterone is NOT standard ED practice; defer to OB/GYN for outpatient consideration in recurrent loss.
- **Bed rest is NOT recommended** (ACOG 2018). No evidence of benefit and may cause harm (VTE risk, psychological distress, lost productivity).
- **Pelvic rest:** Avoid intercourse, douching, and tampon use until bleeding resolves (expert consensus; limited evidence).
- **Rh(D) immune globulin:** 50 mcg MICRhoGAM IM for Rh-negative patients at < 12 weeks; 300 mcg RhoGAM IM at >= 12 weeks. See Critical Actions note regarding 2024 ACOG update on < 12-week administration.

**Inevitable or Incomplete Abortion (Open Os, Active Bleeding):**

Hemodynamically stable -- three management options (shared decision-making with patient):

1. **Expectant management:** Appropriate for incomplete abortion with minimal retained tissue and light bleeding. Complete expulsion occurs in 80% within 2 weeks. Requires reliable follow-up and patient understanding of warning signs.

2. **Medical management (misoprostol):**
   - Misoprostol 800 mcg vaginally (preferred route for efficacy). May repeat dose in 24-48 hours if incomplete expulsion.

guidance.title: Ectopic Pregnancy
guidance.summary:
**Definition:** Implantation of a fertilized ovum outside the uterine cavity. 95% are tubal (ampullary > isthmic > fimbrial > interstitial). Non-tubal: ovarian, cervical, cesarean scar, abdominal, heterotopic.

**Incidence:** 1-2% of all pregnancies. Leading cause of maternal death in the first trimester.

**Risk Factors:**
- Prior ectopic pregnancy (10-25% recurrence)
- Tubal surgery or ligation (especially electrocautery)
- Pelvic inflammatory disease / STI history
- IUD in situ (does not increase absolute risk, but if pregnancy occurs with IUD, 50% are ectopic)
- In vitro fertilization (2-5% ectopic, 1% heterotopic)
- Smoking
- Age > 35
- Endometriosis
- DES exposure

**Presentation:**
- Amenorrhea or missed period (75%)
- Vaginal bleeding (typically light, dark blood) (80%)
- Unilateral pelvic/abdominal pain (90%)
- Asymptomatic (detected on routine early US — increasingly common)

**Ruptured Ectopic — Surgical Emergency:**
- Sudden severe abdominal pain
- Peritoneal signs (guarding, rebound, rigidity)
- Hypotension, tachycardia (hemorrhagic shock)
- Shoulder pain (diaphragmatic irritation from hemoperitoneum)
- Syncope or near-syncope
- Vaginal bleeding (may be minimal despite massive intraperitoneal hemorrhage)

**Exam Findings:**
- Adnexal tenderness (unilateral)
- Adnexal mass (palpable in < 50%)
- Cervical motion tenderness
- Uterine size less than expected for dates
- Cul-de-sac fullness (hemoperitoneum)

guidance.title: Miscarriage
guidance.summary:
What is a miscarriage? 
 A miscarriage is an unexpected loss of pregnancy before the 20th week. Most miscarriages happen very early in the pregnancy, often before a woman even knows she is pregnant . 

 What causes a miscarriage? 
 A miscarriage can happen in any pregnancy. Most miscarriages occur because the fetus doesn't develop properly. This is often linked to a genetic problem with the fetus, such as an extra or missing chromosome. 

 In many cases, the cause of a miscarriage is unknown. Some possible factors that may increase the chance of a miscarriage can include: 
 
 Problems with the uterus or cervix 
 Chronic diseases, including polycystic ovary syndrome 
 Genetic problems with the fetus 
 Pregnancy after 35 years of age 
 Smoking, drug or alcohol use 
 Certain chronic (long-term) health conditions, such as uncontrolled diabetes 
 Severe malnutrition 
 

 What are the signs of a miscarriage? 
 The signs of a miscarriage may be different for everyone and can vary based on how far along you are in your pregnancy. 

 Signs of a miscarriage can include: 
 
 Vaginal spotting or bleeding with or without pain. Some women may have some spotting in early pregnancy and don't miscarry. To be sure, contact your provider right away if you have any bleeding. 
 Dark-colored vaginal discharge. 
 A gush of fluid or tissue from your vagina. 
 Cramping or pain in your abdomen (belly) or lower back. 
 

 Sometimes, it's hard to know what's normal during pregnancy. If something seems unusual or is worrying you, talk to your provider. 

 How is a miscarriage diagnosed? 
 To check if you have had a miscarriage, your provider may do the following: 
 
 A pelvic exam to check your cervix. 
 Blood tests to check things such as the amount of blood loss and confirm pregnancy .

 Abdominal (belly) pain 
 Shoulder pain 
 Vaginal bleeding 
 Feeling dizzy or faint 
 

 How is an ectopic pregnancy diagnosed? 
 An ectopic pregnancy can't be diagnosed without blood tests and an ultrasound . Your health care provider will do a pregnancy test to confirm that you're pregnant. They may do a pelvic exam to check for areas of pain, tenderness, or a mass.

 An ectopic pregnancy needs treatment to stop any damage to your organs. Your provider will use medicine or surgery to take out the ectopic tissue.

 Uterine fibroids or polyps 
 Hormone problems 
 Hormone pills, such as birth control pills and hormone therapy for menopause 
 Cancer of the cervix , ovaries , uterus or vagina 
 Thyroid problems 
 

 Bleeding during pregnancy can have several different causes. It is not always serious, but to be safe you should contact your health care provider right away.

### Definition
Premature separation of a normally implanted placenta from the uterine wall after 20 weeks' gestation and before delivery. Occurs in 0.5-1% of pregnancies.

### Classic Presentation
- Painful vaginal bleeding (70-80% of cases)

1. **Excluding abruption because vaginal bleeding is minimal or absent.** 20-30% of abruptions are concealed. Severe pain, uterine rigidity, hemodynamic instability, and fetal distress with minimal visible bleeding is concealed abruption until proven otherwise.

2. **Relying on ultrasound to diagnose abruption.** Ultrasound sensitivity is only 25-50%. A retroplacental clot can be isoechoic with the placenta. Abruption is a clinical diagnosis — ultrasound is useful for excluding previa, not for confirming abruption.

3. **Performing a digital cervical exam before excluding placenta previa.** Digital exam in previa causes hemorrhage. Obtain ultrasound to confirm placental location before any cervical exam.

4. **Under-resuscitating because "she's young and compensating."** Young pregnant women maintain blood pressure until 30-40% blood volume is lost, then decompensate precipitously. Tachycardia and narrowed pulse pressure in a pregnant patient with vaginal bleeding represent significant hemorrhage. Resuscitate aggressively.

5. **Failing to check fibrinogen and coagulation studies.** DIC complicates 10-20% of severe abruptions. Fibrinogen < 200 mg/dL predicts massive hemorrhage. Fibrinogen < 100 mg/dL is associated with postpartum hemorrhage refractory to standard management. Check coagulation panel early and serially.

6. **Not considering trauma and domestic violence.** Abruption is the most common cause of fetal death from trauma. Screening for intimate partner violence is mandatory. Even minor trauma can cause abruption. All pregnant trauma patients require a minimum of 4-6 hours of fetal monitoring.

**Threatened Abortion (Viable IUP, Closed Os):**
- **Expectant management** is standard. No intervention has been proven to prevent progression to miscarriage.
- **Progesterone:** The PRISM trial (Coomarasamy 2019, NEJM) showed no significant benefit of vaginal progesterone for threatened miscarriage overall (75% vs 72% live birth rate, p=0.08). - **Bed rest is NOT recommended** (ACOG 2018). No evidence of benefit and may cause harm (VTE risk, psychological distress, lost productivity).
- **Pelvic rest:** Avoid intercourse, douching, and tampon use until bleeding resolves (expert consensus; limited evidence).
- **Rh(D) immune globulin:** 50 mcg MICRhoGAM IM for Rh-negative patients at < 12 weeks; 300 mcg RhoGAM IM at >= 12 weeks. See Critical Actions note regarding 2024 ACOG update on < 12-week administration.

Hemodynamically stable -- three management options (shared decision-making with patient):

1. **Expectant management:** Appropriate for incomplete abortion with minimal retained tissue and light bleeding. Complete expulsion occurs in 80% within 2 weeks. Requires reliable follow-up and patient understanding of warning signs.

2. **Medical management (misoprostol):**
   - Misoprostol 800 mcg vaginally (preferred route for efficacy). May repeat dose in 24-48 hours if incomplete expulsion.

What is a miscarriage? 
 A miscarriage is an unexpected loss of pregnancy before the 20th week. Most miscarriages happen very early in the pregnancy, often before a woman even knows she is pregnant . 

 What causes a miscarriage? 
 A miscarriage can happen in any pregnancy. Most miscarriages occur because the fetus doesn't develop properly. This is often linked to a genetic problem with the fetus, such as an extra or missing chromosome. 

 In many cases, the cause of a miscarriage is unknown. Some possible factors that may increase the chance of a miscarriage can include: 
 
 Problems with the uterus or cervix 
 Chronic diseases, including polycystic ovary syndrome 
 Genetic problems with the fetus 
 Pregnancy after 35 years of age 
 Smoking, drug or alcohol use 
 Certain chronic (long-term) health conditions, such as uncontrolled diabetes 
 Severe malnutrition 
 

 What are the signs of a miscarriage? 
 The signs of a miscarriage may be different for everyone and can vary based on how far along you are in your pregnancy. 

 Signs of a miscarriage can include: 
 
 Vaginal spotting or bleeding with or without pain. Some women may have some spotting in early pregnancy and don't miscarry. To be sure, contact your provider right away if you have any bleeding. 
 Dark-colored vaginal discharge. 
 A gush of fluid or tissue from your vagina. 
 Cramping or pain in your abdomen (belly) or lower back. 
 

 Sometimes, it's hard to know what's normal during pregnancy. If something seems unusual or is worrying you, talk to your provider. 

 How is a miscarriage diagnosed? 
 To check if you have had a miscarriage, your provider may do the following: 
 
 A pelvic exam to check your cervix. 
 Blood tests to check things such as the amount of blood loss and confirm pregnancy .

 Treatment after a miscarriage often depends on when it occurs during the pregnancy. If you miscarry early in your pregnancy, you may not need any treatment. If you are 12 or more weeks pregnant, you may need a shot to prevent problems with the Rh factor in future pregnancies. 

 In some cases, tissue is left in the uterus. If you don't have any signs of infection, your provider may recommend waiting for the tissue to pass naturally. If you need treatment to remove the tissue, it can include: 
 
 Medicines 
 A procedure called dilatation and curettage (D&C) or vacuum aspiration 
 

 No matter when it occurs, losing a pregnancy can be difficult. Counseling may help you cope with your grief. Later, if you decide to try to get pregnant again, talk with your provider to understand any risks. Many women who have a miscarriage go on to have healthy pregnancies later. 

 Can a miscarriage be prevented? 
 Miscarriage can affect anyone and often can't be prevented. Focus on taking good care of yourself and start prenatal care visits early in your pregnancy.

3. **Using the discriminatory zone as a definitive rule-out.** A single hCG below the discriminatory zone does not exclude ectopic. Ruptured ectopics have been reported at hCG levels as low as 10-100 mIU/mL. The discriminatory zone guides ultrasound interpretation, not clinical decision-making.

4. **Confusing a pseudosac with an IUP.** A pseudosac (decidual reaction to ectopic pregnancy hormones) appears as a small intrauterine fluid collection without a double decidual sign, yolk sac, or fetal pole. Misidentifying this as an IUP delays ectopic diagnosis. A true IUP has a yolk sac or embryo.

5. **Dismissing a stable patient as low-risk.** Ectopic pregnancies rupture without warning. Patients who are hemodynamically stable in the ED can rupture hours later. Clear return precautions, reliable follow-up, and understanding of warning signs are mandatory.

6. **Anchoring on declining hCG.** A falling hCG does not eliminate rupture risk. Ectopic pregnancies can rupture while hCG is declining, including after methotrexate treatment. Pain in a patient with known ectopic and declining hCG still requires urgent evaluation.

**Definition:** Implantation of a fertilized ovum outside the uterine cavity. 95% are tubal (ampullary > isthmic > fimbrial > interstitial). Non-tubal: ovarian, cervical, cesarean scar, abdominal, heterotopic.

**Incidence:** 1-2% of all pregnancies. Leading cause of maternal death in the first trimester.

**Risk Factors:**
- Prior ectopic pregnancy (10-25% recurrence)
- Tubal surgery or ligation (especially electrocautery)
- Pelvic inflammatory disease / STI history
- IUD in situ (does not increase absolute risk, but if pregnancy occurs with IUD, 50% are ectopic)
- In vitro fertilization (2-5% ectopic, 1% heterotopic)
- Smoking
- Age > 35
- Endometriosis
- DES exposure

**Presentation:**
- Amenorrhea or missed period (75%)
- Vaginal bleeding (typically light, dark blood) (80%)
- Unilateral pelvic/abdominal pain (90%)
- Asymptomatic (detected on routine early US — increasingly common)

**Ruptured Ectopic — Surgical Emergency:**
- Sudden severe abdominal pain
- Peritoneal signs (guarding, rebound, rigidity)
- Hypotension, tachycardia (hemorrhagic shock)
- Shoulder pain (diaphragmatic irritation from hemoperitoneum)
- Syncope or near-syncope
- Vaginal bleeding (may be minimal despite massive intraperitoneal hemorrhage)

**Exam Findings:**
- Adnexal tenderness (unilateral)
- Adnexal mass (palpable in < 50%)
- Cervical motion tenderness
- Uterine size less than expected for dates
- Cul-de-sac fullness (hemoperitoneum)

chunk.text:
What is an ectopic pregnancy? 
 The uterus, or womb, is the place where a fetus grows during pregnancy . In an ectopic pregnancy, the fertilized egg grows in the wrong place outside the uterus. It usually occurs in the fallopian tubes. These tubes carry eggs from the ovaries to the uterus. Sometimes, an ectopic pregnancy can occur in the ovaries, abdominal cavity, or the lower part of the uterus (cervix). 

 Ectopic pregnancies can't end in a healthy pregnancy because the egg cannot grow. If the pregnancy continues, the fallopian tube can burst. This can cause internal bleeding, which can be a life-threatening emergency that needs immediate surgery. 

 What increases my risk of an ectopic pregnancy? 
 An ectopic pregnancy often happens because there is a problem with your fallopian tubes. But sometimes it's not clear why an ectopic pregnancy happens. 

 Factors that may increase your risk for an ectopic pregnancy can include: 
 
 Previous ectopic pregnancy 
 Prior pelvic, abdominal, or fallopian tube surgery 
 Certain sexually transmitted infections (STIs) 
 Pelvic inflammatory disease 
 Endometriosis 
 Becoming pregnant while using an intrauterine device (IUD) for birth control 
 Becoming pregnant after a tubal ligation 
 

 Other factors that may increase your risk can include: 
 
 Smoking 
 Being older than age 35 
 Infertility treatments 
 

 What are the symptoms of an ectopic pregnancy? 
 You may not notice any symptoms at first. Or you may have some of the usual signs of pregnancy such as a missed period , breast tenderness, or nausea.

 Shoulder pain

1. **Call the OB emergency team immediately.** OB, anesthesia, OR nursing, neonatology. Activate massive obstetric hemorrhage protocol. This is not a workup-first scenario.

2. **Two large-bore IVs (16-gauge or larger).** Rapid crystalloid bolus 1–2 L warmed LR or NS. Draw: CBC, type and crossmatch (4 units pRBC), BMP, PT/INR/PTT, fibrinogen.

3. **Supplemental oxygen via non-rebreather mask.** Continuous maternal pulse oximetry and fetal heart rate monitoring.

4. **Activate massive transfusion protocol** if hemodynamic instability present. Do not wait for lab confirmation. Transfuse O-negative pRBC until crossmatch complete; target 1:1:1 ratio (pRBC:FFP:platelets).

5. **Do NOT delay surgery for imaging.** Diagnosis is clinical. In a hemodynamically unstable patient with suspected uterine rupture, immediate laparotomy is the only diagnostic and therapeutic intervention. Ultrasound may be used at the bedside in stable patients only.

6. **Urgent cesarean delivery** — the only definitive treatment. Delivery via laparotomy (classical midline incision for speed in emergency). Extract fetus and placenta.

7. **Uterine repair vs. hysterectomy** — decision made intraoperatively based on extent of rupture, patient hemodynamic status, and desire for future fertility. Repair is preferred if feasible; peripartum hysterectomy is definitive for uncontrollable hemorrhage or complex multi-site rupture.

8. **Neonatal resuscitation team at bedside** — fetal outcome is time-dependent; neonatology must be present at delivery.

9. **Terbutaline 0.25 mg SC or IV** — may be given as a tocolytic temporizing measure to reduce uterine contractions if immediate OR is not yet available, but do NOT delay surgery for this.

Menstruation , or a period, is a woman's monthly bleeding. Abnormal vaginal bleeding is different from normal menstrual periods. It could be bleeding that is between periods, is very heavy, or lasts much longer than usual. It also includes bleeding that happens before puberty or after menopause. Causes can include: 
 Uterine fibroids or polyps 
 Hormone problems 
 Hormone pills, such as birth control pills and hormone therapy for menopause 
 Cancer of the cervix , ovaries , uterus or vagina 
 Thyroid problems 
 

 Bleeding during pregnancy can have several different causes. It is not always serious, but to be safe you should contact your health care provider right away. 

 Pelvic exams, blood tests, imaging tests , and other procedures can help your health care provider diagnose the problem. Treatment depends on the cause. Treatments may include medicines, hormones, and surgery.

**Definitions and Classification:**
Early pregnancy loss (miscarriage) refers to nonviable intrauterine pregnancy up to 13 weeks 0 days gestational age. Classification by clinical presentation:

- **Threatened abortion (O20.0):** Vaginal bleeding with closed cervical os and viable intrauterine pregnancy (IUP) on ultrasound. Fetal cardiac activity present. Occurs in 20-25% of all pregnancies; approximately 50% will progress to pregnancy loss.
- **Inevitable abortion:** Vaginal bleeding with open (dilated) cervical os. Membranes may be intact. Pregnancy loss is imminent or unavoidable.
- **Incomplete abortion:** Partial expulsion of products of conception (POC). Open os, ongoing bleeding, retained tissue on ultrasound.
- **Complete abortion:** Complete expulsion of all POC. Bleeding diminishing. Os closing or closed. Empty uterus on ultrasound with prior confirmed IUP.
- **Missed abortion / embryonic demise (O02.1):** Nonviable pregnancy retained in utero. Closed os, minimal or no bleeding. Diagnosed on ultrasound (absent fetal cardiac activity or anembryonic gestation).
- **Spontaneous abortion, unspecified (O03.9):** Completed pregnancy loss without further specification.

**Incidence:** 15-20% of clinically recognized pregnancies end in spontaneous abortion. The true rate including preclinical losses is 30-50%. Most occur in the first trimester (< 13 weeks).

**Risk Factors:**
- Advanced maternal age (risk doubles from age 20 to age 35; exceeds 50% after age 45)
- Prior miscarriage (recurrent loss defined as 3 or more consecutive losses)
- Chromosomal abnormalities (cause 50-60% of first trimester losses; most common: trisomies, monosomy X, triploidy)
- Uterine anomalies (septate uterus, fibroids, Asherman syndrome)
- Uncontrolled diabetes or thyroid disease

1. **Failing to check a pregnancy test.** Every reproductive-age female (roughly 12-55) with abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, syncope, or hypotension needs a pregnancy test. Ectopic pregnancy occurs after tubal ligation, with IUDs, and in patients who report no sexual activity. The test takes 3 minutes and the miss kills.

2. **Assuming an IUP excludes ectopic in IVF patients.** Heterotopic pregnancy (simultaneous IUP + ectopic) occurs in up to 1:100 in assisted reproduction, compared to 1:30,000 in natural conception. Always evaluate the adnexa in IVF patients regardless of IUP status.

3. **Using the discriminatory zone as a definitive rule-out.** A single hCG below the discriminatory zone does not exclude ectopic. Ruptured ectopics have been reported at hCG levels as low as 10-100 mIU/mL. The discriminatory zone guides ultrasound interpretation, not clinical decision-making.

4. **Confusing a pseudosac with an IUP.** A pseudosac (decidual reaction to ectopic pregnancy hormones) appears as a small intrauterine fluid collection without a double decidual sign, yolk sac, or fetal pole. Misidentifying this as an IUP delays ectopic diagnosis. A true IUP has a yolk sac or embryo.

5. **Dismissing a stable patient as low-risk.** Ectopic pregnancies rupture without warning. Patients who are hemodynamically stable in the ED can rupture hours later. Clear return precautions, reliable follow-up, and understanding of warning signs are mandatory.

6. **Anchoring on declining hCG.** A falling hCG does not eliminate rupture risk. Ectopic pregnancies can rupture while hCG is declining, including after methotrexate treatment. Pain in a patient with known ectopic and declining hCG still requires urgent evaluation.

| Ectopic pregnancy | No IUP on TVUS; adnexal mass or free fluid; hCG above discriminatory zone with empty uterus. Must be excluded in every patient with first trimester bleeding. |

**Threatened Abortion (Viable IUP, Closed Os):**
- **Expectant management** is standard. No intervention has been proven to prevent progression to miscarriage.
- **Progesterone:** The PRISM trial (Coomarasamy 2019, NEJM) showed no significant benefit of vaginal progesterone for threatened miscarriage overall (75% vs 72% live birth rate, p=0.08). A subgroup with history of >= 3 prior miscarriages showed benefit (72% vs 57%). Routine progesterone is NOT standard ED practice; defer to OB/GYN for outpatient consideration in recurrent loss.
- **Bed rest is NOT recommended** (ACOG 2018). No evidence of benefit and may cause harm (VTE risk, psychological distress, lost productivity).
- **Pelvic rest:** Avoid intercourse, douching, and tampon use until bleeding resolves (expert consensus; limited evidence).
- **Rh(D) immune globulin:** 50 mcg MICRhoGAM IM for Rh-negative patients at < 12 weeks; 300 mcg RhoGAM IM at >= 12 weeks. See Critical Actions note regarding 2024 ACOG update on < 12-week administration.

**Inevitable or Incomplete Abortion (Open Os, Active Bleeding):**

Hemodynamically stable -- three management options (shared decision-making with patient):

1. **Expectant management:** Appropriate for incomplete abortion with minimal retained tissue and light bleeding. Complete expulsion occurs in 80% within 2 weeks. Requires reliable follow-up and patient understanding of warning signs.

2. **Medical management (misoprostol):**
   - Misoprostol 800 mcg vaginally (preferred route for efficacy). May repeat dose in 24-48 hours if incomplete expulsion.

**Definition:** Implantation of a fertilized ovum outside the uterine cavity. 95% are tubal (ampullary > isthmic > fimbrial > interstitial). Non-tubal: ovarian, cervical, cesarean scar, abdominal, heterotopic.

**Incidence:** 1-2% of all pregnancies. Leading cause of maternal death in the first trimester.

**Risk Factors:**
- Prior ectopic pregnancy (10-25% recurrence)
- Tubal surgery or ligation (especially electrocautery)
- Pelvic inflammatory disease / STI history
- IUD in situ (does not increase absolute risk, but if pregnancy occurs with IUD, 50% are ectopic)
- In vitro fertilization (2-5% ectopic, 1% heterotopic)
- Smoking
- Age > 35
- Endometriosis
- DES exposure

**Presentation:**
- Amenorrhea or missed period (75%)
- Vaginal bleeding (typically light, dark blood) (80%)
- Unilateral pelvic/abdominal pain (90%)
- Asymptomatic (detected on routine early US — increasingly common)

**Ruptured Ectopic — Surgical Emergency:**
- Sudden severe abdominal pain
- Peritoneal signs (guarding, rebound, rigidity)
- Hypotension, tachycardia (hemorrhagic shock)
- Shoulder pain (diaphragmatic irritation from hemoperitoneum)
- Syncope or near-syncope
- Vaginal bleeding (may be minimal despite massive intraperitoneal hemorrhage)

**Exam Findings:**
- Adnexal tenderness (unilateral)
- Adnexal mass (palpable in < 50%)
- Cervical motion tenderness
- Uterine size less than expected for dates
- Cul-de-sac fullness (hemoperitoneum)

What is a miscarriage? 
 A miscarriage is an unexpected loss of pregnancy before the 20th week. Most miscarriages happen very early in the pregnancy, often before a woman even knows she is pregnant . 

 What causes a miscarriage? 
 A miscarriage can happen in any pregnancy. Most miscarriages occur because the fetus doesn't develop properly. This is often linked to a genetic problem with the fetus, such as an extra or missing chromosome. 

 In many cases, the cause of a miscarriage is unknown. Some possible factors that may increase the chance of a miscarriage can include: 
 
 Problems with the uterus or cervix 
 Chronic diseases, including polycystic ovary syndrome 
 Genetic problems with the fetus 
 Pregnancy after 35 years of age 
 Smoking, drug or alcohol use 
 Certain chronic (long-term) health conditions, such as uncontrolled diabetes 
 Severe malnutrition 
 

 What are the signs of a miscarriage? 
 The signs of a miscarriage may be different for everyone and can vary based on how far along you are in your pregnancy. 

 Signs of a miscarriage can include: 
 
 Vaginal spotting or bleeding with or without pain. Some women may have some spotting in early pregnancy and don't miscarry. To be sure, contact your provider right away if you have any bleeding. 
 Dark-colored vaginal discharge. 
 A gush of fluid or tissue from your vagina. 
 Cramping or pain in your abdomen (belly) or lower back. 
 

 Sometimes, it's hard to know what's normal during pregnancy. If something seems unusual or is worrying you, talk to your provider. 

 How is a miscarriage diagnosed? 
 To check if you have had a miscarriage, your provider may do the following: 
 
 A pelvic exam to check your cervix. 
 Blood tests to check things such as the amount of blood loss and confirm pregnancy .

 Abdominal (belly) pain 
 Shoulder pain 
 Vaginal bleeding 
 Feeling dizzy or faint 
 

 How is an ectopic pregnancy diagnosed? 
 An ectopic pregnancy can't be diagnosed without blood tests and an ultrasound . Your health care provider will do a pregnancy test to confirm that you're pregnant. They may do a pelvic exam to check for areas of pain, tenderness, or a mass. 

 What is the treatment for an ectopic pregnancy? 
 An ectopic pregnancy needs treatment to stop any damage to your organs. Your provider will use medicine or surgery to take out the ectopic tissue. 

 Losing a pregnancy can be devastating. An ectopic pregnancy is like a miscarriage , but it must be treated to prevent problems. People cope with grief in different ways.
